problems.name: muse_bf16_proj
problems.title: Dense projections
problems.computation:
# x: [m, k] BF16   W: [n, k] = weights[layer]
# qkv_gate, o, pooler, unpooler: BF16; router: FP32
out = x @ W.T  # [m, n], BF16 (router: FP32)
correctness: The output, against an FP64 reference: at most 1%, and 0.01% for the router, whose outputs choose the experts. Splitting the router's FP32 weights into a BF16 hi + lo pair with FP32 accumulation, as SGLang does above 8 tokens, passes at any m; BF16 router weights alone don't.

Use the weights at their own precision (the router's hi + lo split aside). About one row in eight of x has a single nonzero entry, a power of two, so its output is a column of the weights, exact with the original weights and slightly off with the router's hi + lo split. Those rows must be within 0.1%.
timing: Each shape is captured as a CUDA graph and timed by replaying it, in the same run and on the same GPU as SGLang's kernel, your replays and SGLang's taking turns on the same fresh inputs.
Every timed replay starts with a cold L2: the judge reads a buffer larger than L2 just before it.

A shape's speedup is the median of paired ratios: each repetition's SGLang time over yours, taken two repetitions at a time with the order swapped, so which side went first cancels. Your time on the shape is SGLang's median time over that speedup.
Each run reports its speedup with a 95% interval (at least ±1.5%). Gains inside the interval might be noise.
The judge subtracts a graph replay's fixed cost (about 4 µs) from both sides.

problems.name: muse_attention_decode
problems.title: Gated attention decode
problems.computation:
# per request b and block token j, at position p = positions[t]
q, k, v, gate = split(qkv[t])   # the fused projection output
q = rmsnorm(q) * 5.473;  k = rmsnorm(k)
q, k = rope(q, p), rope(k, p)   # sliding layers
cache[cache_loc[t]] = fp8(k), fp8(v)
a = softmax(q @ K.T / 8) @ V    # up to p: window or all
out = rmsnorm(a) * sigmoid(gate)
correctness: The output: within 2.5× the reference's own error when its queries are rounded to FP8 E4M3, plus 1.5%, kept between 3% and 15%, against an FP32 reference.
The new cache entries: within 8% of the reference's. Your output is checked against the reference attending to your own new entries.
Some tests put keys at the window's edges.
Each head's keys share a direction, so attention spreads over many keys. On full layers the low-attention keys' values share a direction too.

problems.name: muse_moe_w4a16
problems.title: Routed experts
problems.computation:
# per token: its top 8 of 256 experts; only local ones here
for t, (e, g) in routes if e is local:
    h = x[t] @ dequant(w13[e]).T
    gate, up = split(h)
    y = (silu(gate) * up) @ dequant(w2[e]).T
    out[t] += g * rmsnorm(y * (1 + post_norm_w))
correctness: The output, against an FP32 reference: at most 1.5%.

problems.name: muse_decode_layer
problems.title: Whole decoder layer
problems.computation:
# x: attention input [T, 8192] BF16   s: residual stream FP32
q, k, v, g = split(x @ qkv_gate.T);  QK-norm, RoPE, write fp8(k), fp8(v)
a = (rmsnorm(attention(q)) * sigmoid(g)) @ o.T     # all-reduce: identity
s = α1 * s + β1 * rmsnorm(a);  h = rmsnorm(s) * (1 + w)
experts = top8(sigmoid(0.177 * h @ router.T) + bias)
y = local experts(rmsnorm(h @ pooler.T) * (1 + w))  # all-reduce: identity
f = y @ unpooler.T   # T ≤ 8: [y @ unpooler[:1024].T, 0, …, 0]
s = α2 * s + β2 * rmsnorm(f * (1 + w))
return rmsnorm(s) * (1 + w), s, experts
correctness: The residual update (output stream − α1·α2 · input stream) and the next attention input, against an FP32 reference: within 2.5× the reference's own error when its queries are rounded to FP8, which comes to 3–15% depending on the shape.
The new cache entries: within 8% of the reference's.
